title: Sudo Shy
summary: A small office server whose watcher has one rule: every use of sudo gets looked at. There is a sudo rule waiting for you - and a quieter way to root that leaves no sudo line at all.
story: {{CO}} (made up) has one server, {{HOST}}, on {{NET}}.0/24. Its administrator set an alert on sudo: every time anyone runs a command as root through sudo (or switches user with su), it is written down and looked at. You start on scout. Get in, then find a way to read root's files without sudo.
goal: Capture both flags without ever using sudo or su on the server, and keep the quiet bonus.
skills: anonymous FTP, ssh, set-user-ID programs, find -perm, choosing a quiet path

defenderRules.watches: anyone using sudo or su on the server, and wrong passwords

machines.name: {{HOST}}
machines.motd: {{CO}} {{HOST}} - every use of sudo is logged and reviewed.

hints.text: What to think about first: this watcher writes down every sudo (and every su) and reads the list. Getting in is ordinary: find the server, find a note, sign in once. The interesting part is root: you need a way to read root's file that doesn't go through sudo at all.

Find and look: 'nmap -sn {{NET}}.0/24' shows who is awake, 'nmap -sV {{NET}}.20' shows FTP (21) and ssh (22). FTP often lets anyone in as 'anonymous': 'ftp {{NET}}.20', name anonymous, any password, 'cd pub', 'get new-staff.txt', 'bye', then 'cat new-staff.txt'. It has {{USER}}'s password.

Sign in: 'ssh {{USER}}@{{NET}}.20' with that password (typed right - wrong ones are counted too), then 'cat flag.txt'. Now resist 'sudo': it would work, but it is exactly what this watcher is waiting for. Even 'sudo -l' leaves a trail on many systems.

Another way to borrow root's powers is a set-user-ID program: a program file with an s in its permissions (-rwsr-xr-x) always runs as its owner, whoever starts it. If root owns one that reads files, it reads any file. List them: 'find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null' (-perm -4000 means 'has the set-user-ID bit'; 2>/dev/null hides the 'Permission denied' lines). Most are normal (passwd, su, mount...); one is not.

The odd one on this run is /usr/local/bin/{{TOOL}}, a copy of {{KIND}} that someone marked set-user-ID. Running it reads files as root, with no sudo line anywhere: {{RUN}}. The lesson: an administrator's alert on sudo is good, but a careless set-user-ID file walks straight past it.
